subject: system-design
title: Design Typeahead Suggestion
summary: Suggest the top completions for whatever a user has typed so far, in well under 100ms. Precompute ranked completions into a cached trie instead of ranking live on every keystroke.

blocks.text: Typeahead suggests the most likely completions as the user types each character. The challenge is latency: a suggestion has to come back faster than the next keystroke, so the whole design is built to make a lookup a cheap cache hit rather than a live ranking computation.

items: Functional: given a prefix, return the top-k completions for it.
Suggestions ranked by popularity (how often each completion is queried).
Latency under ~100ms end-to-end, so it keeps up with typing.
Fresh enough that trending queries appear within hours, not instantly.

blocks.text: Every keystroke is a request, so query volume is several times search volume, easily hundreds of thousands of lookups per second. The space of distinct prefixes is large but bounded, and the answer for a given prefix changes slowly. That mismatch between an extreme read rate and slow-changing answers is exactly what makes precomputation and caching pay off.

Store completions in a trie keyed by prefix, where each node caches the top-k completions that pass through it. A lookup walks the trie to the node for the typed prefix and returns its cached list. That costs O(length of the prefix), independent of how many completions exist beneath it.

items: A trie maps each prefix to its node; every node stores its precomputed top-k completions.
A query service walks to the prefix node and returns the cached top-k.
An offline pipeline aggregates query logs and rebuilds the trie with fresh popularity counts.
An in-memory cache (and the trie itself) keeps hot prefixes a single fast lookup away.

blocks.title: Why suggestions are precomputed offline
blocks.text: Ranking completions live on every keystroke would mean scanning and sorting all matches per request, which is far too slow at this read rate. Instead, a batch job aggregates query frequencies from logs and bakes the top-k into each trie node ahead of time. The result barely changes minute to minute, so paying once offline and serving a cached answer is the right trade.

An offline pipeline reads aggregated query logs, counts how often each query was issued, and walks every completion up its prefixes, keeping the top-k at each node. The freshly built trie is then published to the serving fleet. Updates happen hourly or daily on a schedule, not on every keystroke, so the serving layer is read-only and fast.

A global trie is too big for one machine, so shard it by prefix, for example by the first character or two, and route each lookup to the shard owning that prefix. Layer a cache in front so the hottest prefixes never even reach a shard, and replicate shards to spread the enormous read load and survive node failures.

blocks.title: Read-only serving is the win
blocks.text: Because the serving path never writes, you can replicate and cache it freely and scale reads almost without limit. All the messy aggregation lives in the offline pipeline, keeping the latency-critical path simple.
